## 3. Drawing a hypothesis test (30%)

Suppose we conduct an experiment to measure the effect of a new mood-boosting drug.
Patients are randomly assigned to take either the new drug or a fake drug for three months.

-   Let $\hat{p}_1$ be the proportion of patients in the new drug group who report an improved mood.

-   Let $\hat{p}_0$ be the proportion of patients in the fake drug group who report an improved mood.

-   As it turns out, $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_0 = 0.2$.

We conduct a two-sided hypothesis test of $H_0: p_1 - p_0 = 0$, where $p_1 - p_0$ is the true difference in the proportion of patients who would report an improved mood if they took the new drug, relative to if they took the fake drug.
We use a significance level of $\alpha = 0.1$, and calculate a two-sided p-value of $0.15$.

a. Draw a diagram illustrating this hypothesis test. Label each of these seven components:

    1. The null sampling distribution of the estimator. You can assume the CLT is satisfied by the choice of estimator and sample size.
    2. The value of the estimand under the null hypothesis.
    3. The estimated standard error of the estimator under the null hypothesis. You do not have to compute it, just label it.
    4. The area corresponding to $\alpha$.
    5. The bounds of the $H_0$ rejection region. You do not have to compute the bounds, just label them.
    6. The observed value of the point estimate.
    7. The area corresponding to the two-sided p-value of the test.

    Your picture does not have to be drawn to scale, and you are free to use shortened labels like [1], [2], [3], etc. Make your labels and annotations BIG AND CLEAR!

b. Now suppose that the true difference is $p_1 - p_0 = 0.1$. In other words, if we were to give the real drug to the entire patient population in one universe and give them the fake drug in the other universe, the true difference in the proportion of patients who report an improved mood with the real drug versus the fake drug would be $0.1$.

    -   Draw the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_0$ in a world where $p_1 - p_0 = 0.1$. You can assume its standard error of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_0$ is the same as the standard error in your drawing from part (a).

    -   On the same axis, also draw the null sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_0$ from part (a).

    -   Shade the area of the true sampling distribution corresponding to the parallel universes where we obtain a point estimate that leads us to reject the null hypothesis.

    How should we interpret this area? What is this area called? *Hint: See the Lecture 17 worksheet.*

## 4. Many experiments (15%)

A large number of randomized experiments were conducted to determine whether taking a particular drug regularly would decrease the chance of getting a certain disease.
For each of the experiments, the drug effect is the difference between the proportion of people taking the drug who got the disease and the proportion of people taking a placebo who got the disease.
In each experiment, $\alpha = 0.05$.

Suppose the drug had no true effect. Answer each of the questions below. Then, write an explanation of at least one sentence, or make one drawing, to justify your answer.

a. Fill in the blank: We expect p-values to be less than 0.05 for \_\_\_\_% of experiments.

b. True or false: There will be a similar number of experiments showing positive and negative values of the drug effect.

c. Fill in the blank: When 95% confidence intervals for the true effect are constructed, those confidence intervals will include 0 about \_\_\_\_% of the time.

## 5. From confidence intervals to hypothesis tests (15%)

Suppose the 95% normally-approximated confidence interval for the proportion of voters who will vote for candidate A in the upcoming election is $[0.51, 0.59]$.

a. What is the two-sided p-value for the corresponding hypothesis test of $p_{H_0} = 0.5$?

b. If we assume the researchers used $p_{H_0}$ in their calculation of the margin of error, what was the sample size needed to construct this confidence interval?

Make sure your answer includes `pnorm(...)` and/or `qnorm(...)` as needed. If you choose to use `pnorm(...)` or `qnorm(...)`, run your computation in R and report the numeric output with appropriate precision.
